title: Don't Believe What You Read In The Product Details
text:
So I thought this hose would be different from all of the other "horror stories" I had read about other hoses of this type. If you read the details in the description, they suggest you will get about "1200 uses" out of this hose compared to "250 uses" from other similar hose manufacturers. And the brass ends looked like quality in the product photos. Well I thought I would probably never need it for 1200 uses, since this would be a very limited use hose stored inside in a boat and would only be used occasionally to rinse the boat off, so I made the purchase.

I had used the hose only 10 times over the span of three years (2017-2020) prior to the last time I "tried" to use it. It had always only been stored in the mesh bag and out of the sunlight in an interior cabinet when not in use. This final time, just as soon as I attached the hose end to the hose bib and turned the water on, it sprung a leak right at that connection. Finding no way to even temporarily repair the hose, I disconnected it and went without. At first, I thought maybe the rubber gasket had fallen out, but nope, it was there when I removed the hose from the bib.

So the promise of getting 1200 uses of this hose didn't even live up to what they reported as their competition's numbers of 250 uses. So I realize the warranty is only good for one year, but after my experience with this hose, I would never buy another one. The idea is great, but the technology isn't anywhere near being able to perfect the quality needed to meet their claims of ruggedness. It just won't last that long.

title: Great game
text:
I am kind of surprised at the poor ratings this game received from other reviewers. I agree with all the reviewers that there are quite a lot of bugs in this game. That part of is granted. No arguments there whatsoever. And I have no idea why this game should have so many bugs when Still Life I did not.

However, the way Still Life I ended was perfect in my opinion, since it added suspense to the storyline and it was a good marketing strategy on the part of Microids if you really give it some thought. They are basically telling you - "You want to know what happened afterward? Then buy our next game!" I think that part of it was brilliant. Nothing to be ridiculed at. However, in the end, for whatever reason, the gamers did not like it. So, ultimately the strategy seems to have failed. But, I don't blame Microids for believing it will work. Any reasonably sane business person in the gaming world would have thought it will work.

As for the completing the Still Life I storyline in this game, I do not see how it can be an after thought when they explicitly indicated from the very beginning that that was not the main focus of this game. I think the intention was pretty clear here. From the very beginning of the game, Microids pointed out that they are bringing in a new investigation, and that this new investigation will be the main focus of this game. When they have clearly indicated that from the very beginning, they obviously cannot do things to take that focus away. So, I personally feel that the Still Life I storyline was completed in this game in the appropriate and if I may say so "PERFECT" manner.

And the new investigation storyline was perfect, much more suspenseful than the first, and to be entirely honest, a little more nerve-wrecking for the weak heart. The music fit the scenes perfectly well, and the game had everything it could possibly have to make a reasonable civilian sick to his/her stomach, what with all the gruesome murder scene, photographs and videos. I do not see how Microids could have done a better job with this.

It is way too easy for some gamer who loves shooting games to come play this and say - "Hey I hate this game. It stinks." That is because these types of gamers do not know anything about this type of genre for a game. In all honesty, that is precisely what is wrong with the other reviews here. It is severely biased and unfair because it has been reviewed by an entirely different genre of gamers. It is also way too easy for any gamer, regardless of genre, to come out and say - "This story stank. It was stupid. That stank. This stank. This game is not worthed." It is much harder for writers to write a good story, for gamers to design a good game, and for game manufacturers to put everything together in a good way. We live in a world where everyone believes they are writers. That is the problem. That is why we have so many blogs full of nonsense. Not everybody is, and can be. My point is that this story was written by an "ACTUAL or LEGITIMATE" WRITER. And I think the writer did a great job of it.

Having said all this, I once again admit that there are plenty of bugs in this game. That part of it was inexcusable, especially from Microids; a company that is damn good at game design. At any rate, I would give this game five stars for fun and four stars overall. Certainly not just one or two stars. That is just harsh judgment. And this game is very reasonably priced and is definitely worth buying for gamers interested in crime-solving games. This is not a game for the weak heart, for kids, or for those interested in action games. This is for those who have a taste for a good murder mystery.

I am not looking for great acclaim here. If anyone is frustrated with my review and disagrees with it, give me all the unhelpful ratings you need to. In fact, I expect it, because of the poor ratings for the game. I am not looking for fame. This is not a popularity contest. If anyone finds my review dis-interesting, it is purely a matter of difference of opinion. I recognize such difference of opinion, and request those who are wondering about buying this game to look at some other good reviews besides mine. And I mean good ones with good criticisms. Not just purely positive ones or purely negative ones. There are very few of them who write a good review, and I am not saying that I am one of them. You have to use your judgment in figuring out what is a good review.

title: A refreshing, encouraging collection of biographies of "no name" missionaries
text:
Larry Sharp’s recent book, The Greatest Missionary Generation: Inspiring Stories from Around the World, picks up stories from lesser know missionaries, most of whom will never be featured in an entire volume from a major publisher. But the anecdotes Sharp shares demonstrate clearly that the major difference between those that give their lives in service to God through international missions and those that don’t is a willingness to go.

Sharp himself served as a missionary in Brazil with his family for several decades. He then spent several decades working with Crossworld, a parachurch organization that emphasizes getting people of all professions into the world with the gospel message, and he has been a leader in the Business as Mission (BAM) movement, which has similar aims. His experience as an administrator put him into contact with a large number of missionaries whose stories he has curated into this volume.

There are several dozen missionaries featured in The Greatest Missionary Generation sorted by general topic in the thirteen chapters of the book. The common thread among them is being born at a time to have experienced World War II, thus coinciding with the generation that Tom Brokaw has famously labeled the Greatest Generation, and that they all seem to have come from seemingly insignificant backgrounds.

The pattern may not be universal in this volume, but many of the mini-biographies Sharp records begin with a summary of the individual’s background. Usually from Nowhere, USA. Most of the stories about people from the hills of Appalachia, small mid-West towns, or unknown areas of Canada. The educational background of these saints is also scant, with many of them going to Bible institutes to get just enough training to be approved by the mission board. Not that they didn’t seem to value training, but that they were chomping at the bit to get onto the field.

Each of these stories is about regular people who made a decision to live as vocational workers for the kingdom of God. That’s the main difference between them and the average person in your local church. And that is a powerful reminder that the key qualification for faithful service is willingness.

Generational analysis has been overdone and is often exceedingly uncharitable. However, the formative experiences of the so-called Greatest Generation unquestionably shaped their view of life. My own grandfather, having served in the US Navy and witnessed the invasion of Iwo Jima (something I did not find out about until his funeral), gave his life in service of the kingdom as a church planter in the mid-Atlantic region. Doing analysis after the fact, I have little doubt that the experience of witnessing the horrors of WWII and experiencing the borderline societal collapse did a great deal to diminish the importance of a profitable career for him. The same seems true of so many of the subjects of Sharp’s biographies.

Thankfully, The Greatest Missionary Generation, does not imply that they are the best generation or the only generation doing missions faithfully. Rather, it highlights the ordinariness of the missionaries and seeks to inspire a greater number of regular people to step out from their comfortable first culture lives to take the gospel to the nations. If these people with unexceptional backgrounds can do such unexceptional things, then there is hope for everyone. The biographies of the workers in The Greatest Missionary Generation are timely because these saints have either gone home to glory or will do so in the very near future. Their races have largely been run, so this is a good time to honor their work and tell their stories. The danger of getting too much praise and attention is, for most of these faithful servants, already gone.

I read this book in an afternoon. It was an excellent way to spend a Sunday, reflecting on God’s faithfulness and the response of regular people in taking the gospel to the ends of the earth. This is a book that would likely be better digested more slowly, perhaps shared a chapter at a time with kids toward the end of the day. There are enough short stories in this book to recharge a pastor’s supply of missionary illustrations or move the local Sunday School missions moment past the same dozen or so big names.

In sum, this is an excellent book. It is well worth the time to read it. It should be part of a local church library, could be an inspiring book to read with a group, and would do well to find its way into the hands of teenagers who are considering what they want to be when they grow up. One of the most attractive aspects of the book is the celebration of some “no name” missionaries. May we get more volumes like this that demonstrate the significant impact that ordinary people being ordinary Christians in cross cultural situations can have for the advance of the gospel. The task of reaching every tribe, tongue, and nation will be completed by faithful people like these, not by big names doing extraordinary things.

NOTE: I received a gratis copy of this volume from the publisher with no expectation of a positive review. This is an edited version of a review from Ethics and Culture.

title: Great for temporary start up
text:
I purchased this greenhouse in 2021. Shipping was good. Product arrived in a reasonable amount of time and was well packaged. I used it to overwinter my outdoor potted plants. It remained under my carport throughout the winter months. It worked great in this setting, since it was shielded for strong winds. The assembly is not difficult, but not easy. I have to admit the first time it was a bit confusing. The instructions are not clear. It helped me to sort the connectors and rods into individual stacks by size and letter. Be careful to locate the letter on the connectors and keep them grouped together. Using one connector in the wrong location can throw the entire frame off. Ask me how I know.
Overall sturdiness of the parts is pretty good. This is a PORTABLE greenhouse. It worked great under shelter of my carport. Using it in an open space will require some serous anchoring. The ground staples and string that comes with it are not sufficient. Also the I suggest using stronger zip ties to secure the shelves. I found this out the hard way. I attempted to use this greenhouse again in the spring of this year for seed starting. I have relocated and no longer have a covered carport. I did what I knew was not the best, but figured it was sufficient anchoring. Unfortunately it did not hold up to a windy day. I think it may have been more of the fact I did not zip the door closed and/or maybe the top rods were not securely attached. I also had not secured the shelves. It appeared the wind was able to get inside with through the door open. The bottom section remained in place, but the top rod was loose. I am not giving up! This thing is pretty durable and great for a tight budget gardener like myself. I have plans to assemble this greenhouse again for the winter. This time I am preparing to securely anchor it and monitor it closely each day. Thanks for providing a decent quality product at an affordable price! I would recommend this greenhouse to my family & friends.

title: The quintessential deck of cards
text:
Fun: A standard deck of playing cards offers an incredible variety of ways to have fun. There are, of course, the different kinds of games you can play. Bidding games, like Bridge; betting games, like Poker; solitaire games, like Klondike; and trick games, like Euchre. These games can be played alone, or with as many as seven people... and, more if you add another deck.
You can also try to build structures (although, the taller your house of cards, the more decks you may need)-- and the Bicycle brand cards are ideal for this activity because of their slick coating. In other words, it's a challenge! And, of course, there's the ol' putting a card in the spokes of your bicycle wheels trick just for the heck of it.
Finally, one of the coolest things you can do with this deck of cards is practice and perform magic tricks. Instructions sold separately. :)
Educational value: As a former 8th grade math teacher, I swear by the educational value of playing cards. From simple games like "War", which teach relative numeric values (a 5 is greater than a 3, etc.), to blackjack and 31, which teach adding, and on to 5-hand draw poker, which teaches probability... even when young player doesn't realize he or she is learning. As an adult, of course, there's always room to learn more about probability and finesse, esp. with social and gambling games like poker and bridge.
Durable: The Bicycle brand cards set the standard of quality for plastic-coated playing cards. They don't bend or crease easily and, treated well, can last for years of normal use. Only casino-style cards like Bee can outlast Bicycles in the plastic-coated class. The most durable playing cards are 100% plastic, like those made by Kem (among others), but Bicycle is a great value for both cost and durability.
General: Bicycle stands as one of the few standard brands against which all other plastic-coated playing cards are judged. They last ten times longer than most decks that cost half the price; the face designs are attractive; the numbers are easily readable. These are my brand of choice when I host a card game.

title: Run large, and probably not much "boosting"
text:
These are Yoga pants with a flare leg. They are long, meaning the do go all the way to the tops of your shoes. For me, I'm 5"5', they just bordered on too long, as the extra material in the flare at the bottom felt cumbersome and in my way when I walked and worked out. I really question the reason for "flare" Yoga pants, anyway, since they are designed to be used while exercising, which means being breathable and unsuitable for physical activity should be important features? I mean, flare pants to work out in? Why? Fashion when you sweat? I, personally, don't get this.

Most importantly, these run very large in my opinion. I am 5"5', 155 and carry all my weight in my hips. I am usually between a medium and a large in most athletic pants, with the large being generally more suitable if I don't want to feel squished. These were simply huge on me, and the extra material felt bulky and in my way. I have a size medium in the same brand, and the mediums fit more or less appropriately, more like a large in most of the other brands I have tried.

These claim to be "butt boosters" which basically means that they have a series of seams to outline the area of your seat, instead of most pants which are a solid material that might, possibly, squash your rear flat. In my opinion, these did nothing to "boost my butt", although my personal trainer and boy friend said that they might possibly see some boosting. In these, however, the size was a problem as 'boosting' requires that the pants fit snugly.

The material is thicker feeling than some other brands I've tried, but that could be because of the extra material due to the size, and the "flare" at the bottom. I, personally, do not like the flare as it requires extra material below the knee, but I guess this works for some. The seams are strong and should hold up well over time. title: Theres cheaper alternatives!
text: This review may seem a little biased, since I don't actually have a SodaStream.  You're probably asking yourself, "Then WTF is this guy writing a review on here for then?"  Let me start by saying that I was a big soda drinker, and to help kick the habit, I started drinking carbonated water.  I was drinking it so much that I looked into getting a SodaStream on here to cut down on the costs.  However, after reading some of the reviews on here, and doing some research on my own, I decided against it.  The main reason was the cost of their CO2 bottles.  Sodastream has made it that you have to use their bottles, and the costs of their little bottles can start to add up.  I have never had their soda, but since I wasn't going to get it to make soda it didn't make sense for me to get one.  Anyways, after doing some research, I decided to get a 5 gallon refurbished keg, a 5 pound CO2 bottle, and all the lines and regulator for about $200, (that included filling the CO2 bottle), from my local home brew store.  They told me that the water would need to be pretty cold for the CO2 to really take effect, so I looked on Craigslist for a little mini fridge that would fit the 5gal keg and the CO2 bottle, however, I ended up just getting a new fridge from Walmart for $150.  So all in all, my initial costs came out to $350 for my setup.  I know that it seems like a lot compared to the basic Sodastream package, but after awhile, those little CO2 bottles are going to add up to way more then my setup.  I am still on my first fill up of CO2 and have gone through almost 50 gallons of Carbonated water and still have over half left in my tank.  Once my 5 lb CO2 tank does run out, I can get it filled for $20 and I'm good to go.  So, if you're big on carbonated water, then this is just a suggestion for you guys that may be considering a Sodastream.  You can look at the costs of their bottles and how many liters of water you will get from each bottle, but I can guarantee you that you will get nowhere near 50 gallons, (and I'm still going) for $20, (actually, the bottle itself cost me about $30 so all in all $50).  Either way, just thought that I would put this out there and give you guys some food for thought.  If your big on soda, most local brew stores have their own soda mixes and you can do the same thing. Either way, if you like the Sodastream design, and the fact that it uses no electricity and are into their sodas, then go for it, but if you want a more cost effective way to get your carbonated water fix in the long run, then do a little youtubing or call your local brew mart and I'm sure that they can steer you in the right direction.

title: Courtesy of Confessions of the UnPublished!
text:
Hold on to your hair-gel we have another Dystopian on our hands.

Let me start by saying that...I don't really like dystopian novels. I can thank 1984, BRAVE NEW WORLD, and THE GIVER for all jading me as a kid. And yet, why is it I always end up reading more dystopian types? I guess because every now and then you run into a good one. And--when they're good, they're usually really good. I loved HUNGER GAMES and the UGLIES series. I'm happy to say that this one can added to the goodies list. : So on to my review already--

The central theme to this novel is control or be controlled. No surprise there; aren't all dystopians that central theme? Where this one exceeded my expectations is Vi. She's the strong, kick-butt female we all want in a novel, especially a novel where the main character has to take down 'the man'. Right away she teams up with Jag--the badboy also in prison for breaking the rules--and the whole novel is kind of their escape/self-discovery kind of a thing along the way. Then there's also Zenn--the goodboy--and Vi's 'match' she left at home. It makes for an excellent plot. And I thoroughly enjoyed it (and Vi's sarcastic personality) the whole way through; it didn't disappoint. My favorite favorite part was the ending. It was intense and I loved it. A cliffhanger all the way, but such a perfectly fitting ending. I can't wait to read book 2 (is there a book 2?).

If anything was lacking it was that the romance wasn't 'knock-your-socks-off'. More like sweet and tender. It was good--don't get me wrong--but it didn't blow me away.

title: Great look at one of the most interesting families in American History
text: The Magnificent Medills covers the story of the Medill Family and the McCormick Patterson Dynasty that shaped the course of journalism throughout the late 18th and early 19th century.  Short of Hearst (who the Medills had many dealings with) the family was one of the most influential in shaping United States journalism.  From the start of the Chicago Tribune to Newsweek the Medills and their decedents redefined the way Americans read newspapers. They were the socialites of their day amassing a tremendous fortune and flaunting it in private railway cars, huge houses and extravagant parties.  McKinney provides a very useful family tree as it gets easy to lose track of so many family relations but at the end of the day an excellent job is done in giving enough time to introduce the family member before moving on to introducing a new person.  I am usually not drawn to the socialite type histories but found this one enjoyable and well done holding my interest throughout the whole book. It is not a long and drawn out analysis of early journalism but really does focus on the families and their relations with one another.  Overall enjoyable and well worth it for those interested in the lives of the wealthy for this time period.

title: UPDATED On 4th and 5th try with Dead Pixels!!!
text:
I purchased 2 of these monitors in December 2012 after seeing the 4.5/5 star reviews on both Amazon and NewEgg.
My intention was to eventually order a 3rd and 4th monitor for a full 4 panel display setup.

I received the first 2 monitors within two days of the order, both packaged in Amazon shipping boxes, with brown paper crumpled as packaging padding. Didn't seem too bad. Plus the monitor boxes themselves have the Styrofoam mold in them.

I first noticed a dead pixel on one of the monitors 2 days after I set it up (when I had a grey screen up). I submitted a Return Request to Amazon and they shipped a replacement immediately. It arrived, I set it up, shipped back the old one, and realized the replacement (which was shipped without an outer protective box) also had dead pixels (different location).

Literally as I went to submit for replacement of the replacement monitor, I checked my initial monitor as well, and discovered a "dying" or almost dead pixel. So I have to return a 3rd monitor now.

I've submitted for 2 more replacements from Amazon, but if they have dead pixels as well, I'm done.

Check you monitors as soon as you get them and again in a week. They seem to have very poor quality control.

The monitor build, brightness, and overall quality seem excellent outside of the dead pixels I'm seeing on 3 of these now.

UPDATE (1/23/13): I've received the 4th and 5th replacement monitor and set both up. Approximately 4 days in, I have NO dead pixels on either one. I'll check again in a week, but maybe we finally have 2 that are going to work OK.

I have returned the first two monitors and the faulty replacement.

Still keeping this as a 2/5 star product because 2 out of 5 monitors worked.

title: BRILLIANT!!
text: I'm not a Yes fan, but if anything would convince me to become one, it would be the quality of this album.  No, it isn't my favorite progressive album, but it is definitely up there, and it is among my top 10 or so albums of all time.  Each of these three songs blows me away like nothing else.  The atmosphere is perfect, the emotion is out of this world, and the playing is probably Yes' peak.  The title track is one of the best sidelong tracks ever, with each of its 18 minutes being essential to the quality of the track.  The use of repetition enhances the atmosphere, and the beautiful keyboard poriton by Rick Wakeman create a force more powerful than all but one Yes song.  Siberian Khatru is the best hard rock song Yes has done.  The melodies simply cannot be beaten.  Steve Howe shows he is the king of progressive guitarists.  But the centerpiece of "Close To the Edge" is And You And I, easily my favorite Yes song, and one of the greatest songs of all time.  Howe's guitar is gorgeous for all 10 minutes, and Jon Anderson has never been so expressive with his vocals.  I could probably go on for pages upon pages on the song, but I'll stop here.  This album is a must have for any collection.  There is so much beauty to be found on "Close To the Edge".  Five stars is too little for this one.  Get it NOW!

title: I'm converted
text:
Sorry Mr Mill Valley, CA...it's too bad you have to completely misunderstand JoyE and pass them off so quickly; your fault for missing out on some stellar, timeless music.
I've only recently become interested in the quirky, but genius music of Ronnie Martin. Buying this CD sealed my fandom. I'll forever be interested in what this man and his synthpop vehicle has to put out.
Ronnie has stated numerous times he doesn't care about genres or styles of music; he cares about songs. And his songs are as finely crafted, laced with hooks, and beautifully realized as they come. The quiet, thin, breathy and sometimes even creepy vocals and melody combine with the surprisingly ironic electronic beeps, whirrs and general synth goodness to transport you to Joy Electric land: where you'll be a refuge from the many lands of mediocrity in music today.
And this 2-CD set is as good an introduction as they come. But if you haven't already, buy JE's latest masterpiece, The White Songbook - which was labored on for over a year and a half.
Whether you hate electronic music as a general rule or not, I'm convinced that everyone needs to hear this album at least once all the way through. Even if you hate JoyE at first, I'm convinced that you'll come back. Like I did.

I happened upon a profile of Equation on NPR when their first album "Hazy Daze" was featured. I was immediately drawn by the samples of their melodic song-writing and ability to develop a song beyond a simple hook and chorus. I immediately got the album (had to order it from Amazon because it wasn't easily available elsewhere) and wore the Album's grooves down for a couple of months.
Two weeks ago I happened upon their follow-up album here, "The Lucky Few," and immediately ordered it. I was apprehensive whether they could followup their great first album with similar work. Rest assured. "The Lucky Few" is a fabulously assured follow-up which extends Equation's range with a little more guitar driven sound. If you like a great blend of folk-rock, strong female lead vocals and inventively melodic song-writing influenced by tradition English folk songs (updated), you will love this album. You will not regret buying this album. Go for it.
By the way, Equation has a great web-site .... My only regret is that after completion of this album, Seth Lakeman left the group which will change their sound and direction going forward.

I live in a mountainous suburban area, where Sprint doesn't provide sufficient coverage causing poor data signal & frequent drop calls. I had tried a variety of boosters, initially the zboost 545 then the Wilson Pro. Installation of the "external" antenna is tricky for both of these. And the included coax cable for the zboost was subpar that I had to upgrade to a higher-quality one.

Anyway, installation for the SureCall was much simpler. No need to mount the "external" antennae / booster, although you must find an area with the strongest signal and try to run the cable as inconspicuously as possible.
I enjoy the contemporary design of the Surecall of the others (which is why it received a 4 star).
The signal amplification / quality is between the zboost 545 and the Wilson Pro, with the Wilson Pro being the best. However, to be fair, both the antenna for the zboost & Wilson were placed in the attic. The Surecall was mounted on a window.

So if you prefer ease of installation & decent design, then the Surecall is a good option.

title: Works perfectly!
text:
Pros: It cleans coffee stains extremely well. Not caustic or extremely hazardous. After use a good rinsing is all that is needed. It's very economical. There's 120 tablets in the container and cleaning is only needed every few weeks.

Cons: None, unless you need something that works in 10 minutes.

I bought these to clean a narrow-mouthed steel thermos we use daily for brewed coffee. In the past I used another cleaner which is no longer available, and have been looking for another cleaning agent for a couple of years. In the meantime, the inside of the thermos had turned black from accumulated stains and deposits.

Nothing I have tried cleaned it well. I avoided a couple of products that may have worked but were covered with warnings strong enough to encourage one to wear a hazmat suit because they were so caustic and poisonous.

This stuff will "irritate the skin and eyes" but is far less toxic, so I thought it was worth a shot.

Before bed I filled the thermos with very hot water, leaving a little space at the top, and dropped in one tablet. After a few minutes I shook the contents thoroughly, then topped off the thermos and sealed the lid.

The next morning I poured out an ugly brown stew. After rinsing the thermos thoroughly, I found the inside to be perfectly clean, except for a little remaining buildup around a small rim at the bottom. A little brushing would likely have removed that bit. I'll do that next time.

Highly recommended!

title: Awesome pool to play with the kids in
text:
First of all, I want to start this off by saying this is the first pool experience I've had EVER outside of baby pools (as far as putting up, maintaining, etc). I'm 34 years old with no experience in anything related to pools or building, etc...

This pool was a piece of cake to put together. My husband and I did it in less than an hour, and honestly, I probably could have done it by myself (MUCH easier with someone helping I'm guessing though!). The ground cloth that it comes with is essentially a super thin tarp, so don't expect it to protect the bottom of the pool from much, to be completely honest. I went and bought a roll of roofers felt (I think that's what its called!) for $21 from home depot and put it under the ground cover just for a little more protection and I'm more confident with that down there for some protection.

We worked for a couple of weeks to get the ground nice and level in preparation for our pool because I'd read how important that is. So after weeks of work, we put up the pool, start to fill it with water, and it seemed okay. However, once the water got to a little higher level, I could see that it is completely NOT level. Like, at all. The instructions say that if that happens, you should drain the pool, move it to another location that is level and start over. No thank you. I know that might not be the smartest move and I'm NOT recommending doing that, but we didn't want to drain (waste!) all the water we'd put in already and so we just continued to fill it, and although crooked, it seems sturdy and there are no visible wall seams on the side that is "down hill" (to put it dramatically!). SO we're going to leave it for this summer then have someone professionally level the area when we put it up next year.

The depth is nice and good to splash around in, swim a little, and just cool off and have fun. Being in Southern California, that's really what we were wanting for the summer when it hits the 100+'s! I got chemical instructions from a local pool supply place and it has stayed crystal clear so far, with VERY little maintenance work on my part. We're just using the filter that came with the pool and it is nice and quiet. Works great so far. As far as filters go, I also purchased those here on amazon for roughly $2 each (they come in packs of two), which is a great deal compared to the $12 that the pool store wanted for each one! :)

All in all, we're very happy with this purchase. Easy to put up, easy to maintain, and sturdy for a soft sided pool. We would definitely purchase again and plan to have one every summer from here on out.

title: Get this book if you want a good balance between Reference and Tutorial
text:
This book is awesome. The authors do a great job of balancing Reference with Tutorials and General Insight. Whatever you do, do not skip the Introduction. It provides some great background then guidance on how to use the book.

I've quitely sat back and watched Silverlight mature at a very quick rate, but we could never trust it for our Line of Business (LOB) apps because the data binding was not there. Now, with RIA Data Services and the new controls we are leaving ASP.NET and AJAX frameworks as quickly as we can.

With the help of this fine book, I was able to build CRUDs and transaction processing code for our existing LOB app in four hours. Four hours and we have replaced what took us a few weeks to write in older technologies. And we are using SL 4, so don't think this book is now outdated. We relied extensively on "Chapter 5-Controls" to employ the native DataGrid. It had all we needed to write production quality code. If we want to really tune the grid with some more obscure attributes we'll just search it up online.

If you want the absolute nth level of reference then do what the rest of us do... search then read it online. This book was never intended to be the end-all reference, just a good balance between Reference, Tutorials, and General Insight. As founding member of our .NET Users Group I will recommend it every chance I get to our members.

title: “Kaboom! --- it’s an explosion.”
text:
What kid doesn’t like to blow things up or see things explode. I know I do. This book explodes from beginning to end with tons of information about explosive experiments, devices and unfortunate incidents. It starts with the invention of gunpowder and fireworks in ancient China, takes us all the way through current day explosions in outer space. Along the way we meet inventors and the stories of how they worked towards finding safer, bigger and better ways to blow up things.

Explosive Experiments is another in Ms. Stephanie Bearce’s series, Twisted True Tales From Science. It appeals to middle grade readers, but young adults and adults as well can learn a lot about the history of explosives. It would be a great tool for middle grade teachers. The end of each chapter contains hands on experiments that can be done at home or school. At the end, there is a good bibliography and list of websites … great for anyone who wants to do further research. It’s an easy read and has lots of cool illustrations.

Read this book. You’ll be blown away!

title: Update, it broke after 1 month, but they replaced it.
text:
[[VIDEOID:823d8d597154160e58cbac54a98fe545]] Update 2: The seller did finally get back to me, and they sent me a new unit. It is now winter, so I cannot test it, but I will see how it works next pool season. I will update my review again after testing.

UPDATE: I've had this for a little over a month now. I noticed after about my 6th time using it, the battery lasted less than 1 hour. Then the next time, less than 30 minutes, then 10 minutes, now it doesn't even come on at all. I have sent several emails to them, no response. I contact them through Amazon, no response. I understand a battery going bad, it happens, but honor your 1 year warranty. Don't ghost me. Unless they get back to me and replace my unit, I do not recommend buying this because you will be stuck with trash if it breaks.

Keep in mind, I’ve never used this type of vacuum before. Before getting this, I used one of those robot vacuums that hooked up to your pool filter, that used water pressure from the pump. I was not impressed with that type of vacuum. The space between the suction hole and the pool bottom was like 1.5” inches, so it didn’t get stuff off the bottom well, and it only went in one direction for like 15 seconds before its gear mechanism would make it change directions. The hose would always get tangled, and I would consider it only 60% efficient. I had to leave it in my pool, and run it every day for 4-6 hours at a time in order to keep my pool bottom clean.

So when I tried this, I was blown away big time. The inlet holes are only a half inch from the pool bottom so it picks up debris very very well. It maintains a direction for more than 30 seconds, unless it hits something, then it automatically changes directions. It has wheel settings to allow you to adjust how easily it turns (random of course) for round pools, or if you want it to stay as straight as possible, for rectangular pools. (however, for my round pool I found that the least amount of movement setting works best) It moves very fast. It doesn’t get caught up in my pool ladder, so I don’t need to remove it. With my old robot vacuum, I had to take out my pool ladder because it would get caught in it, and not bet able to get out.

I have an 18’ round above ground pool. And when I ran my old robot, after 4 hours, it would only pickup 60% of the debris, and it would blow the rest along the edges. When I ran this for 90 minutes, it picked up over 95% of the debris. I am really impressed. It may be less for much larger pools.

But like I said, I never used a cordless, self-powered, vacuum before so I can’t compare it to similar type units. I can only get about 80-90 minutes max run time on a single charge. I have never seen 2 hours, and doubt it could every get 2 hours, so the listing is deceiving. After 60 minutes, I can see it slow down a lot. It does do what it says, that when the battery is running low, it will stop near the edge so it is easy to retrieve. It takes about 5 hours to fully charge it on an empty battery. How does this compare to similar units? I do not know. But 90 minutes seems like more than enough run time for me since it is very efficient, and my pool is only 18'. Might not be as efficient for a 24 or 32' pool.

One draw back however. In the instructions, it says to lift it up using the supplied hook, then hold it near/above the water to let the water drain out before removing. Do not do this. The flaps that keep the debris inside the filter do not work so well, so a lot of the fine debris fall back out into the pool. Instead, use the hook to bring it near the surface of the water, then using two hands, grab either side of it, and lift it out right away, so it drains on your pool deck or grass. Do not lift it out, full of water, using the top grab handle, as you might break it. That top handle is required to change directions. If it hits something, the handle moves forward a little, telling the unit to change directions.

All in all, I LOVE this little thing (about 14” in diameter). I am never using my old pump powered robot vacuum again. I never could justify spending $300 for a robot vacuum for an 18’ pool I only paid $300 for 5 years ago. But if I knew then, what I know now, I would have gotten something like this a long time ago and spent the money. I only need to put this in my pool once or twice a week (depending on pool usage). Or after a storm/weather that blows a lot of debris in my pool, and it keeps the bottom very clean all around, even the edges. I’m kicking my self for all that time I wasted manually vacuuming it, or messing with hoses for my other robot vacuum, that didn’t even work that well.

title: One of the last powerful protest movements...
text:
The world has been dominated by overbearing, greed fueled and power mad religions, armies and monarchies since the rise of humanoids. It goes on to this very day in it's many forms. Some are refined and cloaked in self-righteousness. Others through blunt force evil. The common denominator is always the same: The conquest and subsequent enslaving of the innocent. What inevitably follows is the systematic attempt to destroy those who speak out against the tyranny. Though voices are silenced, the spirit endures. It is a reality the barbarian can never grasp. For it has no soul.

One such voice came in the form of Bobby Sands. The story of 'Hunger' concerns him, but it would be a mistake to believe that he was it's sole bearer. He was a representative of a much larger effort to see a united Ireland join the world of independent and free countries. A cause that stretched from the footsteps of men, women and children to the prisoners of the the notorious H-Blocks.

I had read about the hunger strike in 1987. A book by the name of 'Skylark Sing Your Lonely Song' documented the path taken by it's author, Bobby Sands. Each page of that book was more difficult to turn than the last. It was painful, yet necessary to understand what happened, what series of events that led to the strike.

I had heard rumors of movies under consideration to portray the life and times of the prisoners in the Maze. Over the years, I lost track of what might eventually get made. So when I came across 'Hunger' on Netflix, I was hopeful. Remembering the book, I went into the screening just wanting to see an accurate portrayal. What I found was a matter of fact retelling of the hunger strike without fanfare, special effects or heroic sappy dialogue.

There is an extended, one shot scene that features Sands (Michael Fassbender) and a priest named Father Dominic Moran (Liam Cunningham). The scene is brilliantly written and acted. The banter plods along, darts and sometimes dances until it gets to the heart of the matter. Clearly one of the finest moments in film that I have come across in some time.

The 'supplements' are filled with more on the story and the making of the film. We find out exactly who this 'Steve McQueen' is, hear from the actors and are treated to a BBC piece on the Hunger Strike that was never shown in the United States. I highly recommend these extras.

'Hunger' was crafted in sparse, stark tones by director, Steve McQueen. It is an intense, and direct portrait of a dynamic event that unfolded in the early 1980's. In many ways, it was one of the last powerful protest movements that the world would witness after decades of causes borne of action, not lip service. What had been won will be debated for centuries to come. What was lost, forever mourned by the descendants of freedom.

title: Great introduction to fpv flying
text:
I really like Holy Stone Products. I also own another racing drone called the Bolt Bee, which I also highly recommend. I feel that both drones together give a feeling of true fpv racing. The bolt bee doesn't come with a camera, but is extremely fast and a little more responsive than the Mercury 3, AKA HS230.

I really like this drone. It's pretty fast, has stiff propellers and really powerful Motors. The transmitter feels pretty sturdy in your hands and the LCD display is a good size.

The Mercury 3 is not as agile, especially turning from side to side on the right stick, but the yaw is extremely smooth and almost forces you to use the left stick for aggressive turning.

The camera seems pretty clear, but I'm not an expert so I don't really have an informed opinion on how it rates to other drones. It would be nice if the camera was tilted a little more towards the ground for reference; it seems to be facing "too straight" for me.

I like how the camera and the battery are both modular. I also like that the motors don't need to be soldered; when they need to be replaced the motors plug into the circuit board.

I really like the customer service with Holy Stone, one of the reasons I keep buying their products is because they are customer driven. A knowledgeable and friendly email response usually gets back to me within 24 hours. If I ever have any concerns, Holystone goes above and beyond the minimums. They seem to be really generous with their incentives as well. Some people think that one needs to leave a 5-star review to get an extra battery or something; Holystone is pretty clear; they want an HONEST review so they can help make their product better for their customers. They've saved me a lot of money on extra batteries as well.

Ultimately, I hope the company learn how to combine the Bolt Bee's Speed and Agility with the Mercury 3's fpv and battery life. For now, I'm happy to fly each of them.

text: [[VIDEOID:fb366f5e3299a7ab6fd37934a30f1b7f]] I previously owned a Cuisinart coffee maker and it was great, but after many years of use it began having some issues. Sometimes it wouldn't brew...it would just make a clicking sound. Other times it would only dispense tiny amounts of water and you would have to do this 10-15 times in order to fill your cup. (No, this had nothing to do with de-scaling.) These things didn't happen often...95% of the time it still worked great. But I'd had this coffee maker for probably 5-6 years so I figured I'd just buy a new one. My daughter took the old one to use at work. When buying the new one I obviously looked to Cuisinart because I was so pleased with my previous purchase. This one, however, is a disappointment. The water tank has a small crack in it. It doesn't leak, and it's not in a place that's visible, so I didn't return it. I've since learned the crack is probably due to the fact that the tank is difficult to seat after filling. It's such a pain in the neck that now I just take a pot of water over instead of taking the tank to the sink. I only take it off for cleaning. The part where the k-cups go in has the dumbest design feature ever. It's a hinged two-part lever - you lift the first smaller part and as you pull it lifts the bigger second part. I mean...why??? It makes no sense at all. It's just extra parts; and if the flimsy top part breaks who know if you can still get the rest of it to open. The coffee maker has two heat settings - hot and extra hot. I have ours set to extra hot, but I still have to put my cup in the microwave for 30 seconds if I truly want a hot cup of coffee. But the most annoying thing of all is how SLOW it is. It takes a full one minute and forty seconds to brew a single cup. Relatively speaking I know that's not a long time... but compared to my previous one that took about 30 seconds, it  just annoys me. I've added a video of the slow coffee making experience. If you think it's too painful to watch, just imagine how painful it would be to watch your own slow brew when you're running late for work but want to grab a cup of coffee for the road. And speaking of grabbing one to go, only the smallest travel mugs will fit - even after removing the cup tray. If you have a big travel mug you will have to brew into something smaller then pour it into your larger mug. Everything about this design is a downgrade from my previous Cuisinart. Not very pleased with this purchase.

text: This is by far the best of Jennifer Weiner's books.  It's the perfect mix of humor, sadness and mystery.  I loved every minute of it--with the exception being when poor Kate sang at the memorial--I can't honestly believe that anyone would sing "If You're Happy and You Know it" at a funeral...  At any rate Kate shows the imperfect side of motherhood--the doubts and frustration that come along with suddenly discovering you're responsible for so very much...it's not all just pretty outfits and posing for the camera--it's sleepless nights and episodes of puking and daydreams of how life used to be "before"--and in the midst of all of the insanity of motherhood you have children who you'd do anything for and who you love beyond reason--this is Kate's life.  I loved the fact that Kate got to revisit her past and see a road not taken.  And contrary to some reviewers I enjoyed the unanswered questions at the end of the novel.  Kate was left to face some monumental questions and I think that a pat ending would have been a disservice to the rest of the book.  She was indecisive throughout, why would she suddenly see the light at the end of the book and clearly choose her husband.  I thought it was empowering for her to take time for herself and her children to rediscover this new woman that she has become.  Because in a way you leave behind the woman you once were when you become a mother and you have to mesh your old life with your new one.  She was just beginning to do that at the end of the novel.  If you are a person who loves sweet trite stories you won't enjoy this book.  However if you enjoy real fallible characters who don't always do the "right" thing then you'll love reading this book.  This has utterly changed my opinion of Jennifer Weiner--I applaud her ability to craft such an awesome character and I hope she'll continue Kate's story in another book!

title: Great quad for beginners. Terrible camera.
text:
This is pretty good for a beginner quadcopter.

I really like the fact that it came with 3 total batteries. The one inside the battery bay was 500mah while the 2 spares were 600mah. I have been getting around 9-10 minutes of flight time on each, but that number is without the pop guards, camera, or landing gear on. Not that these pieces weight a while lot, but every little bit counts. The included charger is also excellent because it is capable of charging 4 batteries simultaneously. It does take a little longer to charge 4 at a time than just 1 obviously, but it still only took just under 2 hours to fully charge all 4. This package also included a 4GB microSD card inside the camera and a spare 4GB card. Personally, I'll probably never fill either of them though because I don't plan on using the camera all that much. Lastly, the inclusion of a spare set of propellers is very cool. They say the props are the first to go usually in crashes, but this is my 3rd X5C and the only time any of their propellers broke was when one of them lost signal and was carried up around 200ft and then crashed hard into the ground. Even then they were just bent. They probably still would have worked in a pinch.

This quadcopter is extremely stable. Especially in slow mode. I find myself barely trimming, if at all. Usually it's not even necessary. It is the ultimate beginner quad because it is so stable and easy to fly. The throttle is slightly less touchy than one of my other X5Cs, which is nice. It makes it easier to stabilize and hover. The thing that I like best about flying this thing is that I can literally throw it up into the air and kick up the throttle (not even full throttle), and it will correct its orientation and start to hover. It's so fun to see people's reactions when I just throw it like it's nothing. Flips are super easy as well. Just don't do them in moderate winds because the wind will quickly take off with this little thing and you have no control until the flip is complete. It is easy to lose your bearings when this happens and it can get away from you much faster than you would think. Admittedly, I haven't read through the manual much, but I don't think this one is equipped with headless mode, but to be honest I think you are just cheating yourself of really learning if you're using headless modes anyway, so that wasn't a huge deal for me.

I didn't weight this particular quadcopter, but I have weighed one of my identical quads, and with the prop guards, landing gear, camera, and battery all installed, it only weighed 118 grams, so you are well below half of the required weight limit to register this quad with the FAA.

If you're getting his for the camera, get something else. It takes terrible pictures. I'll post a couple of pictures that were taken from it. It is definitely not the "HD" that they advertise, which is why I'm giving this 4 stars instead of 5. The videos are also very low quality, but still fun to play around with for a little while. I'll also upload a video that was s*** from this on one of my first flights with it. Even if the picture quality was decent, the angle is way too low. You have to fly way above whatever it is you're trying to shoot to get it in frame. Like I said, I've already remove the camera from mine and I'm not likely to reattach it.

Overall, this is a great quadcopter for beginners because of price and ease of use. If you have been on the fence about learning to fly or have just had a slight interest in it, go for it. It will be so worth it and you'll have so much fun flying this thing around and learning how it works. I would highly recommend this quad. Just don't et it for the camera.

I received this quadcopter at a discount in exchange for this honest and unbiased review.

title: Outstanding!
text:
When I find an author whose work I really like, I tend to buy all their books and then space them out, to read over a period of time--prolonging the pleasure. In the case of Carsten Stroud, having started with his most recent book, Black Water Transit, I chased down all his previous books and am taking my time reading them.
Sniper's Moon, Stroud's first novel, is like a fireworks display. It starts off with a bang, then dazzles one with bursts of patterns against a night sky. This look at the inside/outside life of an NYPD sniper, a second generation cop, is a stunning piece of work--insightful, compelling and melancholy.
Managing with great skill to weave together simultaneous plot lines, the narrative takes off in high gear and doesn't let up for a moment. All the characters are fully three-dimensional, even the most minor, and while there is a great deal of violence it doesn't get in the way of the story. And when, roughly at the midpoint of this book, the hero Frank Keogh is accused of killing two fellow cops and takes off to try to unravel things from a distance, there ensues what is one of the best hide-and-pursuit segments I've read in a long time.
While I guessed who was the villain of the piece early on, the author manages to pull off a nice surprise ending that is unexpected.
Some of the writing is beautifully lyrical; the insights into the minds of the men and women involved is refreshingly honest. This is a terrific book.
Very highly recommended.

title: A game of beautiful madness
text:
Changeling: the Lost is my favorite World of Darkness game and one of my favorite roleplaying games. The cover is beautiful to behold and the interior art is evocative of the mood of beautiful madness that is central to the game.

The stories you can tell in Changeling are as marvelous and infinite as dreams can be. You have a fantastic world before you.

This might be a difficult game for a new roleplaying group. I would recommend playing as an ordinary mortal character in a World of Darkness game first to learn the basic rules. Another difficulty is that information is spread throughout the book in such a way that is can be difficult to find what you need. I recommend having two or three copies at the table and trying to keep adequate notes on whatever information you need.

The other books in the Changeling line are worthy editions. I recommend Autumn Nightmares as a follow-up purchase.

I prefer old World of Darkness (Vampire: the Masquerade, etc) over their new World of Darkness descendants in most ways but Changeling: the Lost is an exception (along with Hunter: the Vigil). If you were disappointed by Vampire: the Requiem or Werewolf: the Forsaken you should still give Changeling a try.

title: Sweet, Heartfelt and Full of Holiday Cheer
text:
If there's one lady who knows how to create a broken, battered character in need of redemption, it's this gifted storyteller who does so in a spectacular way, making the redemption won that much sweeter and Inspiring.

Tony DeNunzio and his nephew Jax are the latest occupants of Victory Cottage, a place for healing and new beginnings. But his run-in with early childhood teacher, Kayla Harris, at a point when Tony's patience is wearing thin and Jax is acting out, makes him feel like Pleasant Shores may not be the place for him and his traumątized nephew. Maybe he should just go back home and take the job waiting for him at the VA, but Jax needs time to heal from tragedy and seems to connect with the sweet school teacher.

The year is drawing to a close, and Kayla has little time left to keep the resolution she made at the beginning of the year – to finally get her first kiss. The prospects aren’t very promising in their small coastal town, except for the intimidating new resident of Victory Cottage. But as Kayla welcomes Jax to her classroom and his uncle volunteers with the preschoolers, she realizes there's so much more to the man than his stoic, protective outer shell.

With small-town charm and endearing, inviting secondary characters, this book welcomes the reader with open arms, making her a part of the fabric of this delightful, uplifting story. Whenever I’m in the mood for a wholesome, stirring, emotive read, this wrıter is my go-to, because nobody does poignant, inspirational, feel-good romance like McClaın. A beautiful story with a dash of suspense and filled full of redemption, love, forgiveness and second chances, this is just the thing to remind you of the true spirit of Christmas. Enchantingly sweet, profoundly touching, and remarkably uplifting, this extraordinary story will put your heart in the best of holiday spirıts!

title: Excellent Exposition of an Important Industry
text:
As capitalism continues to evolve and spread itself over more and more aspects of human life, it is inevitable that commercial organizations will find ways to profit from those different activities. One such area is the provision of advice – management consultancy, in other words. What previously might have been sought through social networks and personal contacts is now dominated by what author Pieter Klaas Jagersma calls professional service firms. These he defines as being firms that: “… offer advisory services contracted for and provided to organizations by specially trained and qualified persons who assist the client organization, in an objective and independent manner, to identify management problems, analyze such problems, recommend solutions to these problems, and help when requested in the implementation of solutions (p.19).” In fact, the leading firms in this sector have become world-leading brands, capable of attracting some of the very best graduates from business schools and other high-performing individuals from other areas of the business world. Drawing on extensive research in this industry, with numerous personal interviews over the course of a number of years to draw upon, Jagersma outlines in detail how the very best of these firms are managed and have achieved their success and attempt to sustain that success. He has achieved this goal in full with a book of great clarity, thoroughness and understanding.
Jagersma’s methodology appears to be one that is common in works about business and management, although it is not fully explained here – this is a book that reaches out to a wider readership than just specialists. The author has presumably immersed himself in the industry over a number of years, having conducted many interviews and then organized the data obtained through a process of content analysis. This is an approach that enables an author to arrange the results in a systematic and rational manner that might not always match the complexity and occasionally chaotic nature of large, busy organizations in real life. Management studies are studded with examples of works that explain phenomena very accurately but which fail to predict how other organizations might benefit from the lessons drawn from the data. Jagersma seeks to avoid this problem by dividing the organizations studied into a seemingly comprehensive series of chapters: people development, client development, office management and so forth, along with a consideration of winning the competitive battle. It is this last chapter that probably will be of most interest to readers (apart from those who aspire principally to join one of the companies concerned) and it is suitably lengthy and substantive as a result. Naturally, there is no simple answer: “PSF leadership is the result of effective and efficient management of the right market, of the appropriate approach, and of optimum management of the entire chain of daily activities (p.235).” In other words, it is about getting everything right, all of the time. Some might consider that a daunting task, while others will be at once drawing up lists of activities to identify exactly what will be measured and improved and how. There is certainly enough information and normative content within the book to hope to be able to achieve that task. The author mentions in the opening notes that he removed 80% of the original content of the book to make it clearer and more vital but, even so, it remains quite a long manuscript for a work of this kind. As he says, readers (although not reviewers) can pick and choose between which chapters or sections will be of most use to them.
Professor Jagersma has an extensive track record in business education and in publishing and it is something of a surprise that he did not publish this book with a more well-known publisher (possibly just more well-known to me, in any case). Inspiration Press seems to be a perfectly respectable publisher but the editing is imperfect and some parts of the book organized a little strangely. For example, there is a lengthy list of recommended books and journal articles for further reading. This seems too long and at the same time too general to be of real use and occupies a number of pages. More pages are devoted to a list of websites without any annotation. This is again a little strange and seems unlikely to have been included in a large publisher who would have provided an editor likely to have put more pressure on the number of pages available. Similarly, notes are confined to the ends of chapters and no consolidated list of references is provided. These are minor issues, perhaps but part of the experience of reading a book and therefore relevant. I was sent this book for review and worked with an electronic version so did not have the experience of carrying the book around.
Overall, this is an excellent exposition of a fascinating area of business endeavor and will certainly be studied eagerly by the many people interested in working in this field. I can see it having a much wider readership than is found in the libraries of business schools. It represents an outstanding contribution to understanding the professional services sector and of the ways to manage organizations competitively more generally.

John Walsh, Shinawatra University

title: A Writer for and about "The Middle"
text: After reading the 4+ "Rabbit books" and other Updike novels (many inspired by events in Updike's own life) I was very interested in comparing the novels with a good Updike biography.  If you are like me and wish to learn more about Updike, I am quite sure you will enjoy this Adam Begley biography.  It is well researched and well written.  I found that many of my ideas and thoughts about the real John Updike were reinforced by this book.  Updike really was a decent fellow.  He was a highly intelligent and talented writer and his literary success was both earned and deserved.  From his PA high school to Harvard to the New Yorker and beyond it was boom, boom, boom.  He was a talented man on the move.  Updike always said he was comfortable living and writing about "the middle," the average Americans, not the rich, not the poor but just regular the folk who keep this country going.  The man had such an ability to sit down and write such wonderful prose.  I don't think I have ever enjoyed a recent writers prose as much as Updike.  (I like McCarthy, DeLillo, Kennedy and others but Updike is so frigging smooth and easy.)  I understand he gets hammered by some critics for being too "light", too "in the middle," too wispy.  I say unfair.  We all have our preferences and I choose to enjoy a variety of writing styles.  I think Updike was a classy and and a classy writer.  He never "looked down his nose" at the less intelligent folks in America.  May he rest in peace.

title: What a wild ride!
text:
Premeditated Justice has it all! From police procedural brilliant psychiatrist and a murder conviction, plus a serial killer on the loose where a few people have motive and you don't find out until the very end what happened.

Chris is a troubled man who seems to have had the weight of the world to carry for years and at first you think he's someone quite different than he turns out to be. His loyalty to his sister is admirable and feels very authentic considering the childhood they shared.

Dr. Rankin is the most complex character and it's tough to decipher if she has an agenda or is truly looking out for a family that has suffered poverty, loss and physical and sexual abuse.

The one thing I love about crime books is that you don't always root for the good guy, because they turn out to be the bad guy... not saying that's what happened here, but there is darkness on both sides of these iterations.

Murder is complicated and I loved looking at the human side of it through the eyes of someone who just wanted to have a chance at a normal life.

title: THE ONLY SPRAYER THAT WORKS WITH DIESEL
text:
I use the herbicide Crossbow that comes concentrated in kerosene. I mix it in diesel because that penetrates the bark of bushes & trees (mainly oak & Brazilian Pepper) where water-based herbicides just run off. The reason for saturating the lower bark is that spraying the foliage just kills the leaves and the plant comes right back. On oaks, I spray the base of small branches I don't want. Crossbow seems to translocate outward so it kills the branch only and doesn't affect the rest of the tree, I call it chemical pruning that I use while walking around. For righteous pruning, chainsaw.

I tested a dozen or more sprayers and none held up to diesel except this one. It lasts about a year with daily use until it starts leaking at the handle, I expect just due to wear. DO NOT use the Harris Chemical Resistant sprayer; it will seize in a few minutes because the (Viton?) rubber swells and it just locks up. But that one does hold up to chlorine.

If you're trying to kill Brazilian Peppers, another method is to cut the bush/tree a foot high and IMMEDIATELY brush the stump with glyphosate concentrate (51%); it helps to add about 10% of mineral oil to the concentrate but it doesn't mix well so shake often. Maybe some dish soap would solve that. I brush the entire stump but, if it's large, you only need to brush the outer inch where the cambium layer is. This works about 50% of the time which is the reason for cutting it a foot high. If it does re-sprout it will sprout at the top of the stump so you can try again an inch or two lower. If you'd cut it at ground level you have nowhere lower to go.

Bottom line: I use Crossbow in diesel and this is THE sprayer to use. I had an old Zep sprayer that lasted for years but that one is no longer made and the current ones don't work. So I'm stocking up in case Harris quits making these. Sprayers are like shoes, by the time you realize you found the perfect one, it's no longer made.

As one example among many, Tsung Tsai's advice to "Just do. Don't think" in trying situations where action is needed without emotion or fear, was one particular incident that I completely related to.
"Bones of the Master" is more than the story of Tsung Tsai's escape from communist China and his eventual return to his home ground. It is more than a journey undertaken by two friends into Inner Mongolia forty years later. It is a colourful tapestry of the lessons of Buddisim itself, woven with delicacy, gentleness and profound compassion. To Tsung Tsai you might find yourself wanting to say:

title: Reading Riven is like watching a tight, well-scripted movie.
text:
When an author calls a book "the novel I have always wanted to write" I sit up and take notice. And when the author is Jerry B. Jenkins, and the novel is his 175th book, I know I'm going to read something special. Such is the case with Riven. Its premise is simple and dynamic: a condemned inmate requests his execution be in the form of crucifixion. At first we don't know why or the circumstances leading up to his death-row status, but we certainly want to. Most of the book covers the 17 years of the inmate's life up to this point.

Jerry B. Jenkins has a way of immediately drawing you into a story. From our first introduction to Brady Wayne Darby, a rebellious teen who hates his trailer-park life, we care about him. How will he play the cards he's been dealt? Will he throw a chance at a better life away or take it before it's too late? By the hints we're given, we can imagine his fate, but it doesn't lessen the impact of his story. We're compelled to travel the journey with him as he grows from a troubled boy to a troubled man.

Trading scenes with Brady is Thomas Carey, a pastor who's been unjustly fired from his church and is trying to decide his calling. This isn't the first time he's been mistreated, but through it all he's maintained his trust in the Lord and His plan. Until now. Why does it seem everything goes wrong when all He's trying to do is please God? And why has his only daughter strayed so far from her faith?

From Riven's first chapter we guess Brady will be the one who commits the crime, but we don't know the victim or the hows and whys. It's this unknown that kept me turning pages. When would Brady fall? Was there any chance it wasn't him and someone else was the death row inmate described in the opening?

Reading Riven is like watching a tight, well-scripted movie. The short, dialogue heavy scenes keep up the suspense and reader interest. You might need to muster up a little discipline to read the complete texts of numerous classic hymns found in Riven's pages, but they're in there for a reason so even if you're tempted like I was, try not to skip over them. Ultimately, Riven is a novel that'll keep you awake `til two promising yourself over and over that you'll just read "one more chapter". Even though the intensity ebs and flows throughout the story, it never really lets up.

Like his novel Though None Go With Me, Jenkins shows us years in a character's life rather than days or weeks, but the story never suffers for this. Following Brady through most of his life and seeing how many of his bad choices were simply a result of his horrible upbringing gives us compassion for others like him.

The characters of Riven are real, the concept unique, but I daresay it's the message that will stay with readers long after they close the covers. Jenkins was inspired to write the story over twenty years ago when he studied a crucifix at a Catholic retreat center, and it's clear the Cross is the crux, so to speak, of this inspiring novel. How often have we stuffed our Christianity into a convenient little box and forgotten how much Jesus bore to redeem us? Riven shines light on the reason for our faith---the sacrifice at calvary. And we see the power that message has to change lives . . . even lives some would say are unredeemable.

"The message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God."

Mel Gibson's The Passion showed us the reality of the cross; Riven shows us the humanity.

--Reviewed by C.J. Darlington for TitleTrakk

title: Subpar to my Arc5
text:
I have tried many electric shavers over the years, from Philips to Braun to Panasonic and more. My current favorite razor is the Panasonic Arc5 and it has been my main shaver for the past several years. I was excited to try the new Philips Norelco Shaver 7100. It works both wet or dry, has some fancy features such as SenseIQ, has a pop-up trimmer, and more.

In terms of packaging and product design, the Philips gets 5 stars. The package is high end and the shaver itself is well-made and comes with a fair amount of bells and whistles for the tech savvy consumer. It is lightweight, easy to hold, and simple enough to operate and charge. The associated Bluetooth app seems unnecessary and useless. The battery is easy to charge and holds over one hour of use. Even if you forgot to charge it beforehand, a handy 5-minute quick charge gives enough power for 1 shave.

In terms of performance, this is where it starts to fall short. The power is this razor weaker than other razors that I've used. It is quieter which is nice, but not as strong. I found that I need to go over areas multiple passes to get all the hairs. Also, it does not get as close of a shave in comparison to my Panasonic Arc5 shaver. Later in the day, my stubble would appear earlier than usual. Lastly, the shaving head design is frustrating for reaching areas such as under the nose or near sideburns.

The shaver is easy to clean by washing the opened head under running water. It does not come with any cleaning station or charging stand unfortunately. It does have a cleaning brush.

Overall, it is certainly a decent shaver for under $100 and has some nice features, but I find the overall experience of this rotary shaver to be subpar in comparison to my other foil shavers in terms of shaving performance. This rotary shaver is also very tricky to maneuver in certain areas such as under the nose and near areas you want to keep hair such as a beard style or sideburns.

title: Measure carefully and make sure the specs match your guitar.
text:
Although I did some careful measurements on the post and string spacing on my guitar (and was convinced that the new bridge would match perfectly), this bridge did not work out at all. I was replacing an "Adjust-o-Matic" on my Gretsch, and encountered a few problems.
1) The post spacing was too far off, so I couldn't mount the bridge "as is". I ended up having to drill through the bridge and re-use the posts from the old bridge.

2) The "low profile" bridge design (probably a good feature in some situations) did not work out well on my guitar (I had to adjust the posts WAY up).

3) Even though I believe I had sufficient "break angle" and string tension on the roller sadles, some strings were not staying in the saddles.

4) Last but not least, the string spacing was a bit wider than the original bridge, so the strings did not line up with the pole pieces on the pickups, and the spacing on the neck was different as well.

After all the issues I encountered, I regret buying this bridge, and I ended up going back to the original bridge.

title: The ultimate in flexibility and good sound.
text:
I did not get my Bose Home Speaker 500 on Amazon (bought it at a local Bose outlet store) so not sure if this review makes it in. But none the less:

I am in the process of returning a Yamaha MusicCast 50 that also had very good sound for a table top. I was just getting frustrated with its flakiness (you can see my review for it on Amazon) ... I just cut/paste this part of that review here:
After deciding that the Yamaha was not quite as baked as it could be I stopped into a Bose outlet. I'm generally not a Bose fanboy ... high price for what you get. But this Yamaha is very expensive too. So I took a look and listen of course. I listened to the Bose Home Speaker 500. It looks like the MusicCast 20 ... so smaller than the MusicCast 50. I was skeptical but let me tell you ... It sounded about the same as the MusicCast 50 to me. Also it seemed to have better app integration for me. E.g. It supported Amazon Music in addition to Pandora, Spotify, TuneIn, ... and intriguingly it had Alexa support. So I took it home for a test run.
Like I said, it sounds pretty darn close to the MusicCast 50 so that was good. But it was the app support and easy install that blew me away. The initial setup was flawless and intuitive. Yeah I got the Yamaha up but It took a little head scratching (good thing I'm a bit of techy) ... like really it tells me to connect to a private yamaha network to finish the install AFTER the initial connection on the main network timesout ? .... geese. And then you kinda sit there waiting to see what happens next and then it seems to work ... But man , its not a good setup but was able to get through it. On the Bose it just was one two three done. wow. No private network. Just connect and sign into apps.
The Bose also had more presets (6 vs 3).
But the BIG BIG separator is Alexa. I never used Alexa before so was not biased. I am now an Alexa Fan boy :) !!!
I could just tell it to play my favorite station or genres and Alexa would go off and find the station or music where it could find it. It defaults to Amazon Music for music search but you can have it default to Pandora/Spotify etc.
Now its like ... who needs preset buttons?! It totally changes the ease of use and flexibility of the device. Not the least of which is its a full Alexa implementation .... so "Alexa , whats the weather today?" :) :)
